I put a few hours into the game that aren't reflected on steam, so this is a review as of roughly 5-6 hours played total. I definitely recommend this game, despite some shortcomings I'll discuss later. Upfront, I want to say the developers are very, very actively engaged with the community that plays this game, and they have already addressed a number of issues that I had with the 1.0 release (they are now at 1.1, after several rounds of patches). They clearly are passionate about this project, and I think in the current indie game landscape, this game is worth purchasing at full price to support and applaud the developers for the commitment that is on display.

Pros
- Very cool and distinct art style
- Interesting augment system means different runs feel fresh due to some build variety
- Fun moment-to-moment gameplay
- Great soundtrack
- Decent pacing of rewards
- Better with friends

Cons
- The levels within the biomes feel very similar. Due to the rogeulite nature of the game, there is some upfront grinding of the first few levels and I feel there could be more opportunity for variety in level assets and design, as it can get repetitive in a way that some other rogeulites have avoided.
- It seems like there are a lot of weapons, but  getting a new one to drop in the run and then acquiring the kills to unlock at the start seems like a one two punch in terms of needing RNG over multiple runs. Not a huge complaint, but something to note.
- Lastly, the game has sufficient depth to keep it interesting, but can feel shallow at times when upgrades are purely contributing to increases in shield drops or increased healing from drops. This is not really a game to sink hundreds of hours into solo, it's clearly meant to be a fun co-op experience and I believe it certainly delivers that.

 ArcRunner is easily worth the $20 purchase price and if you're interested in supporting some great indie devs, grab the game with friends and start blasting!

The game runs well on Linux and Steam Deck with Proton.
On Deck, you can get a steady 60 FPS with a power draw of 15W by using the low graphics preset, and on ultra I got an average of 30FPS with a power draw of 25W. Medium with a few tweaks hit the sweat spot for me.

ArcRunner gives you many options of playstyle with multiple weapons, gadgets and characters, but only a few choices were useful.
It has some qualities of life I enjoyed:
[list]
    [*]Information you need, like the energy, ammo and number of dashes are represented close to the aim reticle.
    [*]You can stop the game at any time, and when you come back you will start after the last arena you completed, instead of having to restart the whole run or a level
    [*]The hit detection was local, so when I played with friends from far away, we did not have to deal with latency problems
[/list]
The roguelike mechanics feel shoehorned, kind of way to force a stall in your progress in the game. The grind was not different from an RPG that locks your progress behind a boss, and you need to Sisyphus the area before until you have enough experience to defeat it. By the time you reach world 3, the world 1 that was once challenging and fun becomes just a chore as you are over level for those enemies.
The game has an air of unfinished, some augmentations at the end of each level only say, "skills level 1, level 2, and so on".

The dev team has been busy balancing the game, making more options of equipment viable for your run, tweaking characters and fixing bugs. When you read this, many things will have changed, so I recommend you to try the demo, and see if it is something you will enjoy.

I'm really not sure where to even start with this one. I'd say the game is fun *for a while*, but has some fundamental design failings. 

For a roguelite, it offers very limited variety. There are only three playable classes, one of which takes a considerable amount of time to unlock. Many weapons are redundant or just plain bad, and a handful are so completely overpowered that there's no reason for the rest of the arsenal to exist. For having to unlock the ability to carry heavy weapons, and them requiring special ammo Mass Effect-style, they're really, really underwhelming. You can unlock upgrade slots for your weapons, but the upgrades are mostly trivial with a few exceptions, and heavy weapons don't even get upgrades, making them even worse. Weapons you get are also tied to certain regions that you progress through linearly. Using a weapon enough allows you to get it at the start of your run, which when you combine that with the linear metaprogression, means that the first areas become trivial time-wasters. Roguelites with metaprogression need floor skip options, otherwise you end up in a situation where you're just enduring the tedium of early levels, and playing with a friend doesn't help that stay entertaining, it just results in two+ bored players. To make matters worse, dropped weapons and equipment have no power progression (mostly) meaning that once you find the gear item and start with the weapon you want, you can safely ignore any further dropped gear as its stats do not improve in any practical matter. All that *does* matter is the upgrades you pick at the end of each floor, and while they are beneficial, they're sufficiently bland, not offering up much beyond stat increases with only a handful of exceptions. So you've got a roguelite game where the runs vary on only the most minute level, except for the metaprogression, which is remarkably disinteresting.

When I mentioned before that there are only three playable classes, I've only played with one of them despite going through the game twice, once on normal and once on hard. The Ninja is absolutely overpowered in solo because the AI weren't coded to deal with a lone player going invisible. This is very confusing considering there are only three classes, and only two available at the start. I know it's highly insulting to say this, but did the devs really not playtest their game? It doesn't take much to figure out that the AI completely (and I mean completely) breaks down in the face of no visible players. What's worse is that it's very clear that there's minimal difficulty scaling besides enemy damage and health. Some enemies are obnoxiously hard to deal with, but I never really get the feeling of something new being thrown at me, just different flavors of the same thing. Nothing gets me to change my approach, just the method I use to avoid getting hit (which is usually tapping invisibility on for a half second because that breaks the AI). There are some "challenge" events which do not at all scale up their challenges besides switching over to hard mode which is the most laughably pathetic attempt at difficulty scaling I've seen. Multi-kill 5 enemies becomes 7 enemies. 10 melee kills becomes 13 melee kills. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ riveting.

It astonishes me that it took a post-release patch for them to make the player movement not completely terrible, instead upping things to just slightly terrible. For a game with "runner" in the title, you move remarkably slow, even after the patch to speed you up. You can get used to the controls, but I say "get used to" similarly to how you get used to the controls of something like Space Engineers. This is great when enemies and the environment start using AoE attacks which are *sometimes* telegraphed with a visible circle on the ground, but sometimes the circle is bugged and doesn't appear on certain surfaces. Sometimes the circle is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lying, and you get hit with the AoE when you're very clearly outside of it. On that note, you could probably call this location "Red Barrel City" with the number of things that outright explode when you damage them slightly.

The music is okay, perfectly fitting, but there's absolutely not enough variety to avoid getting repetitive. I suggest listening to each track once or twice, then subbing in your own music. The sound design is okay, though as a sound designer myself, I recognize a lot of the samples they used.

The visual style is quite nice, though many enemy designs tend to blend into the background, and it's unclear if that was intentional or not. Though I will comment that they made the ninja's face mask suspiciously similar to that of Jack's from Ghostrunner.

The story is not why you're here. It's basic, it's boring, it's just barely enough context for what it is that you're doing.

None of the problems I mentioned until now are even remotely as bad as the fact that finishing the game resets all of your metaprogression. I thought I read in a patch that they changed it so this no longer happens, but sure enough my things were all reset after beating it on hard. So to that end, I absolutely cannot recommend this game at the price they're charging. If you're curious, maybe wait for a -75% sale.

There needs to be some UI updates regarding clarity (no damage numbers, enemies can be hard to see, augments can be unclear on their effect) along with movement needing to be smoothed out. This game also needs more content, whether it's more varied augments, more weapon mods, more grenades (gadgets) and characters. This game has a strong structure with fun gameplay, but requires more work to broaden the number of builds and make runs feel more different. With some movement, ui, and content updates (many of which shouldn't take too long to implement if the devs are actively working on this), this has the potential to become one the best action roguelike shooters in the genre.

ArcRunner is a sci-fi themed rogue-lite shooter that aims to capture the same magic as games like Risk of Rain 2 and Gunfire Reborn. Unfortunately, it falls short in terms of depth and gameplay mechanics, especially when compared to the creative freedom offered by Risk of Rain 2.

One of the standout features of Risk of Rain 2 is the ability to experiment with different builds and playstyles on each run. This creates a sense of excitement and replayability that keeps players coming back for more. In contrast, ArcRunner's customization options are limited, with a lack of variety in both weapons and abilities. This not only makes the game feel repetitive, but it also discourages the freedom of expression that players seek in a rogue-lite.

The game's slow speed and minimal loot also contribute to its lack of depth. Risk of Rain 2's fast-paced combat and plentiful loot drops keep players engaged and on their toes. In contrast, ArcRunner feels sluggish and underwhelming in terms of loot drops, which further diminishes the excitement of each run.

Overall, ArcRunner is a game that has potential but ultimately falls short when compared to other rogue-lite shooters like Risk of Rain 2 and Gunfire Reborn. While I had hoped that ArcRunner would fill the void left by Risk of Rain 2, it simply doesn't offer the same level of depth and creativity. For those seeking a new game to keep them busy, I recommend keeping an eye on Hyperlight Breaker, which looks promising in terms of filling that void with its intriguing gameplay mechanics and customizable options.

I haven't played that much yet, but I think I'll probably wait for more patches to keep playing. There's some GLARING issues to me. I hope to change this review one day to a yes, but let me highlight some of these negatives that kept me from enjoying my 4 or 5 runs as much as I had hoped.

1: Weapon swapping between your melee and ranged is awkward. The melee weapon feels like something you shouldn't just keep out in this type of game. It's a button, and most of the time you want to melee, then start shooting again. Having to shuffle around because your melee weapon is still in your hands, then click to fire to swap back to your gun, then start shooting baddies again is one of the most awkward and disjointed things I've tried to wrap my head around. In my head, if my melee weapon is just sitting in my hand, then clicking would melee, which I don't want to do, I want to shoot. So my brain goes "How do I swap to my gun again?" and... I have to click. It's super awkward. Take some notes from Warframe. Either have it be quick melee, where you pull it out, melee, then put it back and it's nice and snappy, or make a dedicated swap between your melee and gun. Instead you kind of went with both, which feels weird. I recommend the first one. Also, pressing R to reload even if your gun is empty while your melee weapon is in your hand does nothing, which makes it feel even worse. When's the best time to melee a couple enemies? When you have to reload, but don't have time. Then you still have to do that awkward shuffle in order to reload again.

2: Enemies need to stand out more. As it is, I have to hunt for where the hell they are. They blend into the background. Everything looks samey, even on Ultra. Enemies should be distinct. Give them neon colors, an outline, a different color palette to the background. SOMETHING. I mostly use the red indicators around me, and guess where they are, or follow their attacks to make them out. I'm not on a POS toaster PC either. I'm running it on a 4k monitor with HDR and on ultra. But I've legitimately gotten hit multiple times because I just plain can't see the enemies.

3: The utilities, like grenades and such, feel useless. Like, beyond useless. They're slow, don't do much, and have super long cooldowns. They don't feel like an asset to my run. I try to use them because I feel like I should, but they honestly don't do jack. The auto turret is the only one that sometimes does something, and even that doesn't really do much other then kill 1 or 2 enemies. They're slow, clunky, and feel awful to use. Something with that kind of CD and augments to make them better shouldn't feel this bad. Grenades should explode faster, things should deploy sooner so I don't feel like I have to throw them when enemies are spawning or they'll just casually walk away. These should be my "Oh ♥♥♥♥" buttons. Lots of enemies? Boom, grenade to wipe some out. Need to reload but I'm surrounded? Boom, shield drone or auto turret. They just don't feel strong, or rewarding.

4: Weapons should have a bit more range. If you're going to make a majority of the AI back away from you constantly, then weapons need more range. If not, and you want to keep the range, enemies should be more aggressive. I find a lot of my time in the game is spent sprinting after enemies that are running away from me. It's annoying. The big guys and the drones seem to do it right, getting closer and trying to overwhelm me, but a lot of those smaller guys like the ones with the pistol or the beam rifle like to hide behind stuff and back away from me if I try to get close. 

5: Add a shop and currency you acquire in a run. If you're going to have something as specific as weapons that are powered up specifically by augments you acquire, the RNG of trying to get a gun that also coincides with the augment you chose, and having them both work out is annoying. It rarely ever happens. The only run I did well on I happened to find a gun that was powered up by the augment I was leveling. This would also work well with how many levels the augments can have, letting you buy more of them and upgrade them to finally hit those cool powerspikes without feeling like you just take Micro Missiles for 20 levels in a row.

Things to note: 
I don't hate it, but I acknowledge there is a lot of room for growth. 
I also acknowledge that that this is sort of from an Indie dev and not some big AAA dev team. 
I will come out and say it: I will draw a lot of comparisons to Risk Of Rain 2, because let's be honest, there was a lot of inspiration drawn from that game. 
I've played a fair amount of RoR2 and was searching for something else similar that had more to offer, i.e. more content to play. THIS AIN'T IT CHIEF. 
There are some aspects that are double-edged swords, both pro & con.

Positives:
-The "Reward" you receive at the end of each "phase" is a nice alternative to looting a chest somewhere on the map
-The soundtrack is nice and fits the overall aesthetic.
-Each character feels unique and fit into the universe

Negatives:
-Levels are linear, not much to explore, and has lead me to feel uncomfortably confined. When I played the demo, I was like ooh look at all these shops, can I go in them? no? damn. Maybe if I shoot this thingy? still no? damn.
-The difficulty incline is quite abrupt and thus limit some gameplay options down to absolutely needing certain items just to make gameplay doable.
-OBJECT PERMANENCE has left me not wanting to play the game for a couple years. Upgrades get wiped, Augments "Rewards" wiped on death with a low chance of having the same choices next run, and your entire progress (hours and hours of grinding the same few levels at a time to build up nanites) get wiped upon the end. Due to the huge ramp up of difficulty with only receiving one upgrade is rough. By the time you reach Eden-1 I feel you need double the upgrades you're allowed if you want to keep up with the still increasing difficulty. 

Everything else about the game is MEH. Combat? Serviceable but kind of janky and slow, especially melee combat unless you're playing the ninja. Eesh!

I bought the game hoping to play with gf, hosted a multiplayer lobby, then wanted to continue playing by myself, but they designed your multiplayer progress to be a different instance than single player for whatever reason. Meaning you have to start over if you initially started in MP then want to go solo. 

This sucks, man. I recommend because the potential is awesome, but totally weighed down by the crushing nihilistic feeling due to the design choices.
